short: A bank in which the Government of India owns more than half the shares, such as SBI, Bank of Baroda or Canara Bank.
kid: Some piggy banks belong to one family, and some belong to the whole town. A public sector bank is the town's own piggy bank, looked after for everyone.
detail: A public sector bank (PSB) is a bank in which the central government holds a majority stake. Most became government-owned through the nationalisations of 1969 and 1980, and a merger drive cut their number from 27 in 2017 to 12 by 2020. PSBs hold a large share of India's deposits and loans, carry policy roles such as priority sector lending and Jan Dhan accounts, and have been recapitalised by the government when bad loans ate into their capital. For investors they often trade as a group, tracked by the Nifty PSU Bank index, and usually sell at lower price-to-book multiples than private banks because of governance and growth concerns. A common confusion: a bank with large public shareholders is not automatically a PSB; the RBI reclassified IDBI Bank as a private sector bank in 2019 after LIC took control.
example: Say the government owns 60 crore of a PSB's 100 crore shares, a 60% stake. If it sells 8 crore shares through an offer for sale, its holding falls to 52 crore shares, or 52%, and the lender stays a public sector bank because the stake is still above 50%.

short: India's 1999 law governing dealings in foreign currency, from overseas remittances and foreign investment to trade payments, administered mainly by the RBI.
kid: When you want to swap your toys with children in another country, there are house rules about how much you can swap and how. FEMA is that rule book for India.
detail: The Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA) governs transactions in foreign exchange and dealings between residents and non-residents. It replaced the much stricter Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA) of 1973 from June 2000 and turned violations from criminal offences into civil ones, punished with penalties rather than arrest. FEMA separates current account transactions, such as trade payments and travel, which are broadly free unless restricted, from capital account transactions, such as foreign investment, borrowing abroad and buying overseas property, which are allowed only within rules set by the RBI and the central government. The Liberalised Remittance Scheme, FDI rules and external commercial borrowing norms all sit under it, and the Enforcement Directorate investigates breaches. A common confusion: FEMA is not a tax law; income tax and tax collected at source on remittances come from separate tax rules.
example: Under the rules as of 2025, the Liberalised Remittance Scheme let a resident individual send up to $250,000 abroad per financial year. Someone who had already remitted $180,000 in that year could send at most $70,000 more under the scheme.

short: Investment by a foreigner to own a lasting, significant stake in a business abroad, such as building a factory or buying a large holding.
kid: A friend from another town does not just buy one glass of your lemonade. She helps build your stand, shares in it, and plans to stay and help it grow.
detail: Foreign direct investment (FDI) is cross-border investment that gives the investor a lasting interest and some influence over a business, unlike portfolio investment, which buys small, easily sold stakes. Under India's rules as of 2025, foreign investment of 10% or more of a listed company's equity counts as FDI, smaller stakes count as foreign portfolio investment, and any foreign investment in an unlisted company is FDI. FDI can be greenfield (building new plants) or brownfield (buying existing businesses), and it brings capital, technology and jobs while being steadier than portfolio flows. India sets a sectoral cap for each industry, the maximum foreign shareholding allowed, and caps and conditions change over time, so check the current consolidated FDI policy. A common confusion: gross FDI inflows and net FDI differ, because net FDI subtracts money foreign investors take out and Indian companies' investment abroad.
example: Say a Japanese firm buys a 15% stake in listed ABC Ltd for ₹300 crore. Because the stake is 10% or more, it is recorded as FDI. Had it bought 8% at the same price, for ₹160 crore, it would count as foreign portfolio investment instead.

short: The two ways foreign investment enters India: the automatic route needs no prior government approval, while the government route does.
kid: Some doors to the playroom are always open, so you can just walk in. Other doors need a grown-up to say yes first.
detail: India's FDI policy lets foreign money in through two routes. Under the automatic route, the investor needs no prior approval from the government or the RBI; it invests and reports the transaction to the RBI through its bank within set timelines. Under the government, or approval, route, the investor must first get clearance from the ministry or department in charge of that sector, applied for through the Foreign Investment Facilitation Portal, which replaced the Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB) when it was abolished in 2017. Each sector's rules say which route applies and up to what stake, and some sectors combine both, allowing a stake up to one level automatically and more only with approval. Routes and limits change through DPIIT press notes. A common confusion: the automatic route is not unregulated; investors must still respect sectoral caps, pricing rules and reporting deadlines.
example: Say a sector allows foreign ownership up to 74% through the automatic route and up to 100% through the government route. A foreign investor wanting 90% of a hypothetical ABC Defence Ltd can take 74% without prior approval but needs government approval to go the extra 16 percentage points.

short: A 2020 Indian rule requiring government approval for any investment from countries sharing a land border with India, widely seen as aimed at China.
kid: Neighbours who share a fence with your garden must ask your parents before they can own part of your lemonade stand. Everyone else follows the usual rules.
detail: Press Note 3 (2020 series), issued by DPIIT in April 2020, amended India's FDI policy so that an entity from a country sharing a land border with India, or whose beneficial owner is located in or is a citizen of such a country, can invest only through the government route. It also covers transfers of existing stakes that would shift beneficial ownership to such investors. The rule came during the COVID-19 market crash to prevent opportunistic takeovers of Indian companies, and in practice it mainly affects Chinese money, slowing deals in electronics, fintech and startups that had relied on Chinese venture funding. Proposals to ease it for small minority stakes or manufacturing have been discussed, so check the current position. A common confusion: routing money through a third country such as Singapore does not escape the rule, because approval depends on who the beneficial owner is.
example: Say a Singapore-registered fund whose beneficial owner is a Chinese company wants 5% of an Indian startup valued at ₹2,000 crore, a ₹100 crore investment. Even if the startup's sector is normally on the automatic route, Press Note 3 means the deal needs prior government approval.

short: A marked-off area where businesses get duty-free imports, simpler rules and, historically, tax breaks, mainly to encourage exports.
kid: Imagine a corner of the playground with its own easy rules, where you can bring in crayons without asking. The children there make lots of drawings to send to other schools.
detail: A Special Economic Zone (SEZ) is a demarcated area treated as outside India's customs territory for trade operations, duties and tariffs. India's SEZ Act, 2005 built on earlier export processing zones, starting with Kandla in 1965. Units inside can import inputs and capital goods duty-free and get single-window clearances, and under section 10AA they received a 15-year phased income tax holiday, which is available only to units that began operations by 30 June 2020. Developers include government agencies and private firms, and IT parks and port-led zones are common. SEZs matter for exporters' costs, for office landlords and REITs that own SEZ campuses, and for trade-policy debates about the scheme's value now that new units get no tax holiday. A common confusion: an SEZ unit cannot sell freely into the rest of India; its sales into the domestic tariff area are treated like imports and attract customs duty.
example: Say an SEZ unit imports components worth ₹10 crore that would otherwise attract a 10% customs duty, saving ₹1 crore of duty. If it later sells finished goods worth ₹5 crore into the domestic tariff area, duty is payable on those sales as though they were imports.

short: The price at which the Indian government promises to buy certain crops from farmers, protecting them if market prices fall.
kid: A kind grown-up promises to buy your apples for at least a set number of coins, even if nobody else wants them. So you are not scared to grow apples.
detail: The Minimum Support Price (MSP) is a floor price announced by the central government before each sowing season for 22 mandated crops, including rice, wheat, pulses, oilseeds, cotton and jute, based on recommendations of the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices. Since 2018-19 the government has set MSPs at least 1.5 times the A2+FL cost of production, which covers paid-out costs plus the imputed value of family labour. MSP only bites where the government actually buys, mainly rice and wheat through the Food Corporation of India and state agencies, so many farmers sell below it. MSP hikes matter for markets because they lift farm incomes and rural demand, feed into food inflation and the food subsidy bill, and shape the RBI's inflation outlook. A common confusion: MSP is not a legal guarantee for every sale, which is why farmer groups demand a law.
example: Say the A2+FL cost of producing a quintal of a crop is ₹1,600. Setting MSP at 1.5 times that cost gives at least ₹2,400 per quintal, a 50% margin over cost. A farmer selling 50 quintals to a procurement agency at that price receives 50 x ₹2,400 = ₹1,20,000.
formula: MSP benchmark (since 2018-19) = at least 1.5 x A2+FL cost of production

short: A state-regulated wholesale market, or mandi, where farmers sell crops to licensed traders through auctions, with set fees.
kid: There is a big farmers' fair where everyone brings fruit to one place and buyers call out what they will give. A small team makes sure the fair stays fair.
detail: An Agricultural Produce Market Committee (APMC) is a body set up under a state's agricultural marketing law to run regulated wholesale markets, called mandis. Farmers bring produce, buyers bid in auctions, and licensed commission agents (arhtiyas) handle weighing, payment and often credit, while the APMC charges a market fee. Agricultural marketing is a state subject, so fees, rules and the number of mandis vary widely. Critics say licensing barriers and stacked charges let intermediaries capture margins; supporters say mandis provide price discovery and assured payment. The e-NAM portal, launched in 2016, links mandis electronically so buyers in one market can bid on produce in another. Analysts watch mandi arrivals and prices as early signals of food inflation. A common confusion: the 2020 farm laws that would have allowed free trade outside APMCs were repealed in 2021, so APMC rules still govern much of the trade.
example: Say a buyer pays a 1.5% market fee and a 2.5% commission on ₹1,00,000 of wheat bought in a mandi. The extra charges are ₹1,500 + ₹2,500 = ₹4,000, so the buyer's cost is ₹1,04,000, which is why mandi charges matter for food prices.

short: India's main rainy season, June to September, which brings most of the year's rain and shapes farm output, rural incomes and food prices.
kid: Every summer big clouds bring lots of rain that helps plants grow. When the rain is good, there is plenty of food for everyone.
detail: The southwest monsoon is the seasonal wind shift that brings India roughly three-quarters of its annual rainfall between June and September, starting with onset over Kerala around 1 June. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) measures it against the Long Period Average (LPA), based on 1971-2020 at about 87 cm; seasonal rain of 96% to 104% of the LPA is classed as normal, below 90% as deficient and above 110% as excess. Because about half of India's farmland depends on rain, a weak or uneven monsoon hurts kharif output, rural incomes and demand for tractors, two-wheelers and FMCG goods, and can push up food inflation. El Nino, a warming of the Pacific, tends to weaken the monsoon, while La Nina tends to strengthen it. A common confusion: the seasonal total matters less than its spread; a normal total can hide damaging dry spells or floods.
example: If the LPA for the season is 87 cm and actual rainfall is 80 cm, rainfall is 80 / 87 = about 92% of the LPA. That falls in IMD's below-normal band of 90% to 95%.
formula: Rainfall as % of LPA = (Actual seasonal rainfall / Long Period Average) x 100

short: India's two main crop seasons: kharif crops grow with the monsoon rains, while rabi crops are sown in winter and harvested in spring.
kid: Some plants like to grow in the rainy summer, and other plants like the cool winter. Farmers plant one group, pick it, then plant the other.
detail: Indian farming runs on two main seasons. Kharif crops, such as rice, maize, cotton, soybean, groundnut and tur, are sown with the southwest monsoon in June and July and harvested from September to November. Rabi crops, such as wheat, mustard, chana and barley, are sown from October to December using soil moisture and irrigation, and harvested from March to May. A short summer season in between, called zaid, grows crops like watermelon, cucumber and moong. Markets track weekly sowing data, official output estimates and MSP announcements for each season, because kharif output drives rice and pulse prices while rabi output drives wheat and mustard oil supply. A common confusion: kharif depends mainly on rain during the season, whereas rabi depends heavily on how well the monsoon refilled reservoirs and groundwater, so one weak monsoon can hurt both harvests.
example: Say kharif sowing covers 1,050 lakh hectares by the end of the season against 1,000 lakh hectares a year earlier. Area sown is up 50 lakh hectares, or 5%, which analysts read as a good sign for output if yields hold.

aliases: Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act
short: India's 2005 law guaranteeing rural households up to 100 days of paid manual work a year on demand; Parliament voted to replace it in 2025.
kid: If a grown-up in a village needs work, the village promises a job, like fixing a pond, and pays for it. It helps when there is no other work around.
detail: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005 (MGNREGA; the scheme under it is MGNREGS) gives every rural household whose adults volunteer for unskilled manual work a legal right to up to 100 days of employment in a financial year, at wages notified for each state. If work is not given within 15 days of a demand, an unemployment allowance is due. Wages go directly into bank accounts. Because it is demand-driven, rising work demand is read as a sign of rural distress or weak private hiring, and falling demand as a sign of recovery; it also props up rural wages and is a large Budget item. In December 2025 Parliament passed a law to replace it with a new rural jobs guarantee, VB-G RAM G, offering up to 125 days with states bearing more of the cost, so check which framework currently applies.
example: Say a household gets 60 days of work at a notified wage of ₹300 a day. It earns 60 x ₹300 = ₹18,000 that year, while using the full 100-day entitlement would have given ₹30,000.

short: A government system that sends subsidies and welfare payments straight into people's bank accounts instead of through middlemen.
kid: Instead of handing sweets to a helper who might drop some on the way, Grandma puts them right into your hand. That way every sweet reaches you.
detail: Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) is India's system, launched in 2013, for paying subsidies and welfare benefits directly into beneficiaries' bank accounts, usually linked to Aadhaar for identity checks. It carries payments such as the LPG cooking gas subsidy, PM-KISAN income support for farmers, scholarships, pensions and MGNREGA wages. Paying the right person directly cuts leakages from fake or duplicate beneficiaries and middlemen, and the government reports large savings from removing such names. For investors, DBT matters because it makes welfare spending faster and better targeted, shapes rural cash flows around instalment dates and changes how subsidies appear in the Budget. A common confusion: DBT is a delivery channel, not a scheme in itself; whether a payment is generous or well designed depends on the scheme it carries.
example: Under the rules as of 2025, PM-KISAN paid eligible farmers ₹6,000 a year in three instalments of ₹2,000. If, say, 9 crore farmers receive one instalment through DBT, the government transfers 9 crore x ₹2,000 = ₹18,000 crore in that round.

short: India's combination of Jan Dhan bank accounts, Aadhaar identity numbers and mobile phones, used to send benefits and payments directly to people.
kid: To get a present to the right child, you need their own box, their name tag and a way to call them. These three together make sure the present reaches them.
detail: The JAM trinity refers to Jan Dhan accounts, Aadhaar and mobile phones working together, a phrase popularised by the Economic Survey 2014-15. Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY), launched in August 2014, opened basic zero-balance bank accounts with RuPay debit cards and accident insurance cover for households that had none. Aadhaar, the unique biometric ID run by UIDAI, verifies who a person is, and mobile phones let them receive alerts and make payments. Together they power Direct Benefit Transfer, cheap digital payments through UPI and wider access to insurance, pensions and small loans. For markets, JAM underpins India's financial inclusion story and the growth of fintech and digital lending. A common confusion: opening an account is not the same as using it; analysts track active accounts, average balances and transactions, not just the headline count.
example: By August 2023 PMJDY had crossed 50 crore accounts holding about ₹2 lakh crore of deposits. That works out to roughly ₹2 lakh crore / 50 crore = ₹4,000 per account on average.

short: The pension promised to Indian government employees hired before 2004: a fixed monthly payment of half the last basic pay, paid from current budgets.
kid: When a helper stops working after many years, the town keeps giving her some coins every month. In the old way, the town paid from today's coin jar without saving up beforehand.
detail: The Old Pension Scheme (OPS) is a defined-benefit pension: a retired government employee receives 50% of last drawn basic pay for life, raised with dearness relief, and contributes nothing while working. It is unfunded, paid from each year's revenues, so its cost grows with longevity and pay revisions. The central government replaced it with the contributory National Pension System for most staff joining from 1 January 2004, and most states followed. Since 2022 several states have announced a return to OPS, which the RBI and economists warn adds large future liabilities. In 2024 the Centre introduced the Unified Pension Scheme (UPS), effective April 2025, an option within NPS that assures 50% of the average basic pay of the last 12 months after 25 years of service, funded by employee and government contributions. A common confusion: UPS is not OPS restored; it is funded and needs employee contributions.
example: Say an officer retires with a last basic pay of ₹80,000 a month. Under OPS she gets ₹40,000 a month plus dearness relief, paid from that year's budget. Under UPS, with 25 years of service and an average basic pay of ₹80,000 over her last 12 months, the assured pension is also ₹40,000, but it is backed by a fund built from contributions.
formula: OPS pension = 50% x Last drawn basic pay (plus dearness relief)

short: Four Indian laws that merge 29 older central labour laws into simpler codes on wages, industrial relations, social security and workplace safety.
kid: Imagine lots of different rule books about how helpers should be treated, each a bit different. Someone tidies them into four clear books that are easier to follow.
detail: India's labour codes are four laws passed in 2019 and 2020 that consolidate 29 central labour laws: the Code on Wages, the Industrial Relations Code, the Code on Social Security and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code. They were brought into force in November 2025, with states framing their own rules because labour is a concurrent subject. Key changes include a uniform definition of wages, under which allowances above half of total pay are added back to wages, raising provident fund and gratuity costs for many employers; a threshold of 300 workers, up from 100, before layoffs or closures need government permission; gratuity for fixed-term staff after one year; and social security for gig and platform workers. A common confusion: the codes do not order a pay cut, but a larger wage base raises PF deductions, which can lower take-home pay.
example: Say an employee's monthly pay is ₹1,00,000, with basic pay of ₹30,000 and allowances of ₹70,000. Under the 50% rule, allowances above ₹50,000, here ₹20,000, are added back, so wages for PF and gratuity become ₹30,000 + ₹20,000 = ₹50,000.

aliases: Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade
hl: department for promotion of industry and internal trade
short: The Commerce Ministry department that writes India's FDI policy, recognises startups under Startup India, and publishes industrial data such as wholesale prices.
kid: In a big school, one teacher helps new clubs get started and welcomes children from other schools who want to join. She also keeps a chart of how busy each club is.
detail: The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, was called the Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion (DIPP) until 2019, when it also took charge of internal trade. It frames India's FDI policy and announces changes through press notes, runs the Startup India programme, oversees the patent and trademark offices, and leads ease-of-doing-business work. Its Office of the Economic Adviser publishes the Wholesale Price Index and the Index of Eight Core Industries, both watched by markets for inflation and industrial momentum. DPIIT recognition lets eligible startups, as defined in its 2019 notification, claim benefits such as self-certification under some labour and environment laws; check the current definition before relying on it. A common confusion: DPIIT recognition does not by itself grant the startup tax holiday; that needs a separate certificate from an inter-ministerial board.
example: Say the Index of Eight Core Industries, published by DPIIT, stands at 160.0 in a month and 164.0 in the same month a year later. Core sector growth is (164.0 - 160.0) / 160.0 = 2.5%.

aliases: Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority
hl: pension fund regulatory and development authority
short: India's pension regulator, which supervises the National Pension System, Atal Pension Yojana and the fund managers that run them.
kid: Some grown-ups put a few coins in a special jar every month for when they are old. PFRDA is the careful guard who checks that the jar keepers keep them safe.
detail: The Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) is India's statutory pension regulator, set up in 2003 and given legal backing by the PFRDA Act, 2013. It regulates the National Pension System (NPS), which is compulsory for most government staff hired after the Old Pension Scheme closed and voluntary for others, along with Atal Pension Yojana for informal workers and the Unified Pension Scheme run within NPS. PFRDA registers and supervises pension fund managers, central recordkeeping agencies, points of presence and the trustee bank, sets investment guidelines and decides exit rules, such as how much of the corpus must buy an annuity. Its rules shape long-term demand for government bonds, corporate bonds and equities. A common confusion: PFRDA does not oversee the EPF, which is run by the EPFO under the labour ministry, nor pension plans sold by insurers, which come under IRDAI.
example: Say an employee puts ₹5,000 a month into NPS for 30 years. Her own contributions total ₹5,000 x 12 x 30 = ₹18 lakh, and her final corpus will be larger or smaller than that depending on the returns her chosen pension fund earns.

short: A specialised, usually government-backed lender that provides long-term money for infrastructure, industry, farming or small businesses where ordinary banks hesitate.
kid: Building a big bridge takes many years and lots of coins. A special helper lends coins for that long wait, when other helpers only lend for a short time.
detail: A development finance institution (DFI) is a lender, usually owned or backed by a government, that finances long-gestation projects such as roads, power plants, factories, farms and small enterprises, which commercial banks find too long, large or risky for their short-term deposit funding. DFIs usually raise money through bonds, government capital and refinance lines rather than retail deposits. India's early DFIs, such as IFCI, ICICI and IDBI, funded industrialisation, but ICICI and IDBI later became banks. Today's all-India financial institutions regulated by the RBI include NABARD for farm and rural credit, SIDBI for small businesses, EXIM Bank for trade and the National Housing Bank, plus NaBFID, set up in 2021 for infrastructure. Global examples include the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank and Germany's KfW. A common confusion: a DFI is not just any state-owned bank; its defining feature is long-term, mission-driven lending, not deposit-taking.
example: Say a DFI lends ₹1,000 crore for a toll road over 20 years with equal yearly principal repayments. It gets back ₹1,000 crore / 20 = ₹50 crore of principal a year, a horizon that a bank funded mostly by one-year deposits would struggle to match.

short: The Indian government ministry that prepares the Budget, collects taxes, manages government borrowing and oversees public sector banks and insurers.
kid: In a family, one person looks after the coin jar, decides what to buy and how much to save. The Finance Ministry does that job for the whole country.
detail: The Ministry of Finance runs the central government's money and is led by the Finance Minister, who presents the Union Budget, usually on 1 February. It works through departments: Economic Affairs (DEA) prepares the Budget, plans borrowing with the RBI, frames capital market policy and houses the Chief Economic Adviser, who writes the Economic Survey; Expenditure controls spending; Revenue oversees the CBDT and CBIC, which run direct and indirect taxes; Financial Services handles public sector banks, insurers and pension policy; and DIPAM manages government stakes and disinvestment. Markets track its fiscal deficit targets, borrowing calendar, tax changes and bank recapitalisation decisions. North Block in New Delhi, its long-time home, is used as shorthand for the ministry. A common confusion: the Finance Ministry sets fiscal policy, while the RBI independently sets monetary policy, such as the repo rate.
example: Say the government plans total spending of ₹48 lakh crore and expects ₹32 lakh crore of receipts other than borrowing. It must borrow the gap of ₹16 lakh crore, its fiscal deficit; with GDP of ₹320 lakh crore, that is 16 / 320 = 5% of GDP.

short: India's 2010s problem of overborrowed companies and banks weighed down by bad loans, each holding back investment and lending.
kid: A friend borrowed too many toys and cannot give them back, so the toy lender has few toys left to lend. Now neither of them can play properly.
detail: The twin balance sheet (TBS) problem, a phrase popularised by the Economic Survey 2016-17, describes the period when large Indian companies, especially in infrastructure, power, steel and telecom, had borrowed heavily during the 2000s boom and could not service their debts, while the banks that lent to them, mostly public sector banks, were burdened by rising non-performing assets. Stressed companies cut investment, and banks short of capital slowed lending, so each balance sheet weakened the other and dragged down growth. The fix combined the RBI's asset quality review of 2015, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code of 2016, large government recapitalisation of public sector banks and corporate deleveraging. By the early 2020s policymakers spoke of a 'twin balance sheet advantage', with cleaner banks and less indebted firms. A common confusion: TBS is unrelated to the twin deficits, which are the fiscal and current account deficits.
example: Say ABC Infra Ltd earns operating profit of ₹100 crore a year but owes ₹150 crore of annual interest. Its interest coverage is 100 / 150 = about 0.67, so it cannot pay in full; once its loan is overdue for more than 90 days, the bank must classify it as a non-performing asset and set aside provisions.

short: A stopgap budget presented in an Indian general-election year, seeking approval to spend for a few months until the new government's full budget.
kid: Before a new class captain is chosen, the old captain gets just enough coins for a few days of snacks. Once the new captain arrives, they make the big plan for the whole year.
detail: An interim budget is presented by the sitting government in a general-election year, when a new Lok Sabha will be in place soon after the financial year starts. It sets out estimates for the full year, but Parliament is asked to pass only a vote on account, which under Article 116 of the Constitution lets the government draw money from the Consolidated Fund of India for a limited period, typically two to four months, until the new government presents a full budget. By convention the outgoing government avoids major tax changes and big new schemes, though this is not legally binding; the February 2019 interim budget, for example, announced PM-KISAN and a tax rebate. A common confusion: the two terms are not the same; the vote on account only approves spending, while the interim budget is the full financial statement.
example: Say a ministry's full-year spending estimate is ₹60,000 crore. A two-month vote on account at one-sixth of the annual amount lets it spend about ₹60,000 crore / 6 = ₹10,000 crore until the full budget is passed.

short: The Indian government's goal of making India a developed, high-income country by 2047, the hundredth year of independence.
kid: Imagine planting a small tree and promising that by a special birthday it will be big and full of fruit for everyone. India has made that kind of promise for its hundredth birthday.
detail: Viksit Bharat 2047, meaning Developed India, is the Indian government's stated aim of becoming a developed nation by 2047, the centenary of independence. It frames many policies, Budgets and NITI Aayog plans covering infrastructure, manufacturing, skills, energy and welfare. In economic terms it is usually read as reaching high-income status by World Bank standards, which requires income per person to rise several times from today's level. Economists estimate this needs real GDP growth of roughly 7% to 8% a year sustained for more than two decades, along with higher investment, more productive jobs in manufacturing and services, and better education and health. For investors the vision signals long-term priorities such as capex, housing, power and defence. A common confusion: Viksit Bharat is a goal, not a scheme or fund; programmes such as PLI and infrastructure spending are the tools used to pursue it.
example: If income per person grows 7% a year in real terms, it multiplies by 1.07^10 = about 1.97 in 10 years and by 1.07^20 = about 3.87 in 20 years. Starting from, say, $2,500 per person, 20 years of 7% growth gives about $2,500 x 3.87 = $9,675, which shows why faster or longer growth is needed to reach high-income levels.
formula: Future income = Current income x (1 + g)^n, where g is the annual real growth rate and n is the number of years

short: India's self-reliance policy drive, launched in 2020, to make more at home through incentives, local-purchase rules and support for domestic industry.
kid: Instead of always borrowing crayons from friends, you learn to make your own and maybe share some with others. That is what being self-reliant means.
detail: Atmanirbhar Bharat, Hindi for self-reliant India, is the policy campaign announced in May 2020 alongside a COVID-19 relief and stimulus package billed at ₹20 lakh crore, about 10% of GDP. It aims to strengthen domestic manufacturing and supply chains so India depends less on imports in strategic areas such as electronics, defence, pharmaceutical ingredients, solar equipment and semiconductors. Tools include production-linked incentive (PLI) schemes, preference for local suppliers in government purchases, defence lists that ban imports of chosen items over time, and higher customs duties on some goods. Investors track it through sectors that benefit, such as electronics manufacturing services, defence and capital goods. A common confusion: Atmanirbhar Bharat is not a call to close the economy; the stated aim is to build capacity at home while staying open to foreign investment and exports, though critics say tariff increases echo old-style import substitution.
example: Say a PLI scheme pays 4% on incremental sales over a base year. If a hypothetical ABC Electronics Ltd raises its eligible sales from ₹500 crore to ₹800 crore, it earns 4% of ₹300 crore = ₹12 crore in incentives.

short: Updating the reference year and basket behind an economic statistic, such as GDP or CPI, so it reflects how the economy looks today.
kid: If you keep measuring your height against a mark drawn when you were tiny, it stops being useful. So you draw a fresh mark on the wall and measure from there.
detail: A base year revision updates the reference year, weights, items and data sources behind an index or national accounts series. Statistics such as GDP, the Consumer Price Index (CPI), the Index of Industrial Production and the Wholesale Price Index are built around a base year whose structure goes stale as spending patterns, industries and prices change. Revisions bring in new survey results, so food might get a smaller weight in CPI or services a bigger share of GDP, and they can shift measured growth or inflation. India moved GDP to a 2011-12 base in 2015, and in 2026 the statistics ministry, MoSPI, began releasing new series, including CPI with base 2024 and GDP with base 2022-23. Analysts use back series or linking factors before comparing old and new numbers. A common confusion: a jump or drop in an index caused by rebasing is not real growth or inflation.
example: Say a basket cost ₹2,000 in the old base year and costs ₹2,300 today, so the index reads 2,300 / 2,000 x 100 = 115. If the base moves to a year when the same basket cost ₹2,200, today's index becomes 2,300 / 2,200 x 100 = about 104.5, though today's prices have not changed at all.
formula: Index = (Cost of the basket at current prices / Cost of the same basket in the base year) x 100

short: Spending by households in villages and small towns on everyday goods, vehicles and services, watched as a gauge of India's consumer health.
kid: When farmers have a good harvest, they have more coins to buy new shoes and sweets. When the harvest is poor, they buy less.
detail: Rural demand is consumer spending by households outside cities, where most Indians live. It depends on farm incomes, which swing with the monsoon, crop prices and MSP; on rural wages and construction jobs; on government transfers such as PM-KISAN and MGNREGA; and on money sent home by family members working in cities. Analysts track it through tractor, two-wheeler and entry-level car sales, FMCG volume growth in rural markets, rural wage data and MGNREGA work demand. Weak rural demand, often called rural distress, hurts consumer goods makers, two-wheeler companies and lenders active in villages. Urban demand, driven by salaries and discretionary spending, can move differently, and a split where one recovers while the other lags is sometimes called a K-shaped recovery. A common confusion: higher crop prices do not automatically lift rural demand, because landless labourers and other net buyers of food lose when food prices rise.
example: Say rural markets bring in 40% of a hypothetical ABC Consumer Ltd's sales volume. If rural volumes rise 10% while urban volumes stay flat, total volume grows 0.40 x 10% = 4%.

short: Offices that multinational companies own and run in countries like India to do their own technology, engineering, analytics and finance work.
kid: A big toy shop far away opens its own workshop in your town, where local helpers build and fix toys just for that shop. They do not make toys for anyone else.
detail: A global capability centre (GCC) is an offshore unit that a multinational owns and staffs itself to do work for its global operations, such as software development, engineering and R&D, data analytics, cybersecurity, finance and accounting, risk and HR. Earlier called captive centres or global in-house centres, they began as low-cost back offices in the 1990s and have grown into hubs that own products and decisions. India hosts more GCCs than any other country, with industry estimates putting the number above 1,700 by 2024, concentrated in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai and the NCR. They matter for markets through services exports, white-collar hiring, demand for grade-A offices and office REITs, and competition with IT services firms that might otherwise get the work. A common confusion: in Indian business news GCC usually means this, but in global news it often means the Gulf Cooperation Council.
example: Say XYZ Bank, a hypothetical US lender, pays $200,000 a year per analytics role at home and $60,000 for a similar role in its Indian GCC. Moving 500 roles saves 500 x ($200,000 - $60,000) = $70 million a year, before set-up costs.

short: A panel India's central government appoints about every ten years to recommend new salaries, allowances and pensions for its employees.
kid: Every few years the grown-ups check whether the helpers' coins still buy enough sweets. If sweets got dearer, they give the helpers more coins.
detail: A Central Pay Commission is a body the Government of India sets up, roughly once a decade, to review and recommend pay, allowances and pensions for central government employees and pensioners, and most states later follow its lead. The 7th Pay Commission's recommendations took effect from 1 January 2016, and the 8th Pay Commission was set up in 2025. Between commissions, dearness allowance (DA) for staff and dearness relief for pensioners are revised twice a year using the All-India Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers, to offset inflation. A key number is the fitment factor, the multiple applied to old basic pay to get new basic pay. Pay revisions matter because they swell government salary and pension bills, affect fiscal deficits, and lift spending on cars, durables and housing. A common confusion: a DA increase is not a real pay rise; it only compensates for higher prices.
example: The 7th Pay Commission used a fitment factor of 2.57, so an old basic pay of ₹7,000 became ₹7,000 x 2.57 = ₹17,990, rounded up to the new minimum of ₹18,000. Separately, a DA rate of, say, 50% on basic pay of ₹40,000 adds ₹20,000 a month.
formula: New basic pay = Old basic pay x Fitment factor

short: A policy of making at home the goods a country used to import, usually helped by tariffs, quotas or subsidies for local producers.
kid: Instead of buying cookies from the shop next door, your family learns to bake them at home. Sometimes your cookies are just as good, and sometimes they take more effort.
detail: Import substitution is a strategy of replacing imported goods with domestic production, protected or supported by tariffs, import quotas, licensing, local-content rules and subsidies. India followed it heavily from the 1950s to 1991, building a broad industrial base but also high-cost, low-quality firms shielded from competition, chronic shortages and, eventually, the balance of payments crisis that triggered the 1991 reforms. Modern versions are more targeted: production-linked incentives, phased manufacturing programmes in electronics, defence indigenisation lists and higher duties on selected goods. For companies, import substitution can create protected home markets and fatter margins; for consumers and user industries, it can raise input costs. A common confusion: import substitution differs from export-led growth, which relies on competing in world markets, as East Asian economies did; many countries now try to combine the two.
example: Say India imports ₹1,000 crore of a component a year. If local factories replace 30% of it, imports fall by ₹300 crore, but if the local version costs 10% more, buyers pay an extra 10% x ₹300 crore = ₹30 crore a year.

short: Companies that refine or buy petroleum products and sell petrol, diesel and cooking gas to consumers; in India, mainly state-run IOC, BPCL and HPCL.
kid: A big kitchen turns raw food into ready meals and sells them at its own shops. These companies do the same with fuel for cars and gas for cooking.
detail: Oil marketing companies (OMCs) are downstream oil firms that refine crude oil or buy refined products and sell petrol, diesel, LPG and other fuels through their own pumps and distributors. In India the term usually means the three state-run firms, Indian Oil, Bharat Petroleum and Hindustan Petroleum, which run most fuel stations, alongside private players such as Nayara Energy and Jio-bp. Petrol and diesel prices were freed from government control in 2010 and 2014, but OMCs have often held pump prices steady for long stretches, so their marketing margins swing with crude prices: falling crude widens margins and rising crude squeezes them. LPG sold below cost creates under-recoveries, which the government has compensated at times. OMC shares therefore react sharply to crude prices, the rupee and policy signals. A common confusion: OMCs differ from upstream producers such as ONGC and Oil India, which gain when crude prices rise.
example: Say a fuel cost increase of ₹3 a litre is not passed on because pump prices are held steady. On sales of 1 crore litres a day, a hypothetical OMC's marketing margin falls by ₹3 x 1 crore = ₹3 crore a day, or ₹90 crore over a 30-day month.

short: The shift in how households save, away from gold and property towards bank deposits, mutual funds, shares, insurance and pension products.
kid: Instead of hiding coins under the bed or buying shiny bangles, a family starts putting coins into jars that help shops and factories grow. Over time, those jars give back a little extra.
detail: Financialisation of savings is the gradual move of household savings from physical assets, mainly gold and real estate, into financial assets such as deposits, mutual funds, equities, insurance, provident funds and pensions. In India it has been driven by wider bank access through Jan Dhan, digital payments, easier demat accounts and KYC, and the growth of mutual fund SIPs and NPS. It matters because financial savings can be channelled through banks and markets into business investment and government bonds, deepening capital markets and supporting steady domestic flows into equities that cushion foreign selling. Economists separate gross financial savings from net financial savings, which subtract new household borrowing such as home and personal loans. A common confusion: a fall in net financial savings, as in 2022-23 when it hit a multi-decade low near 5% of GDP, can reflect more borrowing for homes and consumption rather than people saving less overall.
example: Say a family saves ₹3 lakh a year, putting ₹2 lakh into gold and ₹1 lakh into deposits. If it shifts to ₹1 lakh in gold, ₹1 lakh in deposits and ₹1 lakh in mutual fund SIPs, the financial share of its savings rises from one-third to two-thirds.
formula: Net financial savings = Gross financial assets acquired - Financial liabilities incurred
